Situation1: They send an occasional text to check in with their parents over the weekend.
Expectation2: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation2: A friend sends a text message complaining about having a long, boring day.
Story: It’s Saturday afternoon, and I’m sprawled on my bed, scrolling through my phone. I see a message from Mom: “Hope you’re having a good weekend! Miss you.” I know she wants me to reply, maybe even call, just to let her know I’m okay. I haven’t talked to her since Wednesday, and I can almost hear her voice in my head, gentle but a little worried. I start typing a quick reply, but just then, my phone buzzes again. It’s Jamie, my best friend. “Ugh, today sucked. Can I vent?” I know what that means—she needs me to listen, to be there for her, not just with a few words but with my full attention. I stare at both conversations, feeling the weight of what’s expected from me. My parents want reassurance, a sign that I’m thinking of them. Jamie needs comfort, someone to lean on. I can’t do both at once, and I feel the pressure building, torn between being a good child and a good friend, not sure which message to answer first.
